greek_sentence: si enim ita fuisset, non solum laudes aut vitia animorum ad manum aspicerentur, sed etiam disciplinarum scientiae sub oculorum consideratione subiectae non incertis iudiciis probarentur, sed et doctis et scientibus auctoritas egregia et stabilis adderetur ipsique artifices pellicerent sua prudentia, qui, etiam si non pecunia sint copiosi seu vetustate officinarum habuerint notitiam aut etiam gratia forensi et eloquentia, cum fuerint parati, pro industria studiorum auctoritates possent habere, ut eis, quod profitentur scire, id crederetur.
english_sentence_A: For if it had been so, not only would the merits or vices of minds be seen close at hand, but also the knowledge of the disciplines, placed under the scrutiny of the eyes, would be tested not by uncertain judgements; rather, an outstanding and stable authority would be added to the learned and the knowledgeable, and the craftsmen themselves would win favour by their own expertise, who, even if they are not abundant in money, or have not acquired renown through the long standing of their workshops, or even through influence in the forum and eloquence, yet, when they are well prepared, could possess authority in proportion to the diligence of their studies, so that what they profess to know would be believed of them.
english_sentence_B: And to the learned and the knowledgeable an eminent and lasting authority would be added, and the artificers themselves would draw clients by their own expertise. Even if they were not abundant in money, nor had gained renown from the long standing of their workshops, nor even through favour in the forum and eloquence, they could, once they were prepared, hold authority in proportion to the diligence of their studies, so that what they profess to know would be believed of them.

greek_sentence: [3.pr.2] Maxime autem id animadvertere possumus ab antiquis statuariis et pictoribus, quod ex his, qui dignitatis notas et commendationis gratiam habuerunt, aeterna memoria ad posteritatem sunt permanentes, uti Myron, Polycletus, Phidias, Lysippus ceterique, qui nobilitatem ex arte sunt consecuti.
english_sentence_A: [3.pr.2] But we can observe this most of all from the ancient sculptors and painters, because of these, those who possessed the marks of distinction and the favour of recommendation remain in everlasting memory for posterity, such as Myron, Polyclitus, Phidias, Lysippus and the rest, who attained renown from their art.
english_sentence_B: [3.pr.2] We can observe this most of all in the case of the ancient sculptors and painters. Of these, those who held the marks of distinction and the favour of recommendation remain in everlasting memory for posterity: Myron, Polycletus, Phidias, Lysippus and the others who attained renown from their art.

greek_sentence: [3.pr.4] Itaque, imperator, in primo volumine tibi de arte et quas habeat ea virtutes quibusque disciplinis oporteat esse auctum architectum, exposui et subieci causas, quid ita earum oporteat eum esse peritum, rationesque summae architecturae partitione distribui finitionibusque terminavi.
english_sentence_A: [3.pr.4] Accordingly, Emperor, in the first volume I set out for you concerning the art, and what excellences it has, and with what disciplines the architect ought to be furnished, and I added the reasons why he ought to be skilled in them, and I distributed the principles of the whole of architecture by partition and marked them off with definitions.

lsj_entry_text: rătĭōcĭnātĭo, ōnis, f. id., a rhet. and archit. t. t. In rhet. An exercise of the reasoning powers, calm reasoning, ratiocination (opp. impulsio, a passionate feeling, impulse; cf. argumentatio): ratiocinatio est diligens et considerata faciendi aliquid aut non faciendi excogitatio, Cic. Inv. 2, 5, 18: etiam sapientiae studiosos maxime medicos esse, si ratiocinatio hoc faceret, Cels. 1, praef. § 49.— A certain form of reasoning, a syllogism: ratiocinatio est oratio ex ipsā re probabile aliquid eliciens, quod expositum et per se cognitum, suā se vi et ratione confirmet, Cic. Inv. 1, 34, 57; cf.: si ex alio colligitur aliud, nec improprium nec inusitatum nomen est ratiocinationis, Quint. 8, 4, 16; Cic. Inv. 2, 50, 152; Quint. 5, 10, 6; 3, 6, 15; 5, 14, 5 al.— A rhet. figure, reasoning in an interrogative form: ratiocinatio est, per quam ipsi a nobis rationem poscimus, quare quidque dicamus, etc., Auct. Her. 4, 16, 23.— In archit., theory (opp.: fabrica, practice): ratiocinatio est, quae res fabricatas solertiā ac ratione proportionis demonstrare atque explicare potest, Vitr. 1, 1, 1; 15.
greek_sentence: deinde, quod erat primum et necessarium, de moenibus, quemadmodum eligantur loci salubres, ratiocinationibus explicui, ventique qui sint et e quibus regionibus singuli spirant, deformationibus grammicis ostendi, platearumque et vicorum uti emendate fiant distributiones in moenibus, docui et ita finitionem primo volumine constitui.
english_sentence_A: Then, as was the first and necessary matter, concerning city walls, I explained with reasoned arguments how healthy sites are to be chosen; and what the winds are and from which quarters each blows, I showed by linear diagrams; and how the allocations of broad streets and lanes within the walls may be made correctly, I taught, and thus I established the conclusion of the first volume.
english_sentence_B: Next, as was first and necessary, I explained by reasoned arguments, concerning city walls, how healthy sites are to be chosen; and I showed by linear diagrams what the winds are and from which quarters each of them blows; and I taught how the layouts of the avenues and streets within the walls are to be correctly made; and thus I set the limit of the first book.

greek_sentence: proportio est ratae partis membrorum in omni opere totiusque commodulatio, ex qua ratio efficitur symmetriarum.
english_sentence_A: Proportion is the commensuration of a fixed part of the members in every work and of the whole, from which the system of symmetries is produced.
english_sentence_B: Proportion is the commodulation, by a fixed part, of the members in every work and of the whole, from which the principle of symmetries is brought about.

greek_sentence: [3.1.2] Corpus enim hominis ita natura composuit, uti os capitis a mento ad frontem summam et radices imas capilli esset decimae partis, item manus pansa ab articulo ad extremum medium digitum tantundem, caput a mento ad summum verticem octavae, cum cervicibus imis ab summo pectore ad imas radices capillorum sextae, a medio pectore ad summum verticem quartae.
english_sentence_A: [3.1.2] For nature has composed the body of a man in such a way that the face of the head, from the chin to the top of the forehead and the lowest roots of the hair, is a tenth part; likewise the open hand, from the wrist-joint to the tip of the middle finger, is just as much; the head from the chin to the top of the crown an eighth; with the lowest part of the neck, from the top of the chest to the lowest roots of the hair, a sixth; from the middle of the chest to the top of the crown a fourth.
english_sentence_B: [3.1.2] For nature has so composed the body of a man that the face, from the chin to the top of the forehead and the lowest roots of the hair, is a tenth part; likewise the open hand, from the wrist to the tip of the middle finger, just as much; the head, from the chin to the top of the crown, an eighth; from the top of the chest, together with the base of the neck, to the lowest roots of the hair, a sixth; from the middle of the chest to the top of the crown, a fourth.

english_sentence_B: [3.1.6] The mathematicians, however, arguing to the contrary, have said that the number called six is perfect, for this reason: that this number has divisions which, by their ratios, agree with the number six, thus: the sextans is one, the trientes two, the semis three, the bes, which they call dimoiros, four, the quintarius, which they call pentamoiros, five, the perfect six.

greek_sentence: cum ad duplicationem crescat, supra sex adiecto asse ἔφεκτον ; cum facta sunt octo, quod est tertia adiecta, tertiarium alterum, qui ἐπίτριτος dicitur; dimidia adiecta cum facta sunt novem, sesquialterum, qui ἡμιόλιος appellatur; duabus partibus additis et decusis facto bes alterum, quem ἐπιδίμοιρον vocitant; in undecim numero quod adiecti sunt quinque, quintarium, quem ἐπίπεμπτον dicunt; duodecim autem, quod ex duobus numeris simplicibus est effectus, διπλάσιονα .
english_sentence_A: When it increases towards its doubling: with one as added above six, the ἔφεκτον; when eight has been made, which is a third added, the second tertiarius, which is called ἐπίτριτος; when, with a half added, nine has been made, the sesquialter, which is called ἡμιόλιος; with two parts added and ten made, the second bes, which they call ἐπιδίμοιρον; in the number eleven, because five have been added, the quintarius, which they call ἐπίπεμπτον; twelve, however, because it is produced from two simple numbers, the διπλάσιον.
english_sentence_B: As it grows towards doubling, when an as is added above six, it is ephekton; when eight has been reached, because a third has been added, it is the second tertiarius, which is called epitritos; when nine has been reached by the addition of a half, it is the sesquialter, which is named hemiolios; when two parts have been added and ten has been made, it is the second bes, which they call epidimoiros; in the number eleven, because five have been added, it is the quintarius, which they call epipemptos; twelve, however, because it is produced from two simple numbers, is diplasion.

lsj_entry_text: bes, bessis, m. (nom. bessis, Paul. ex Fest. p. 33 Müll.; Prisc. Ponder. p. 1348 P.) [be-is = binae partes assis]. Two thirds of a unit (the as); eight unciae, or twelfths (cf. as): bessis octo sunt unciae (8/12 = 2/3), triens quattuor, Paul. ex Fest. l. l. As a coin: fenus ex triente Idib. Quint. factum erat bessibus, i. e. instead of the previous monthly interest of 1/3 %, 2/3 % was now reckoned; thus, acc. to the present mode of calculating, for the year, the interest advanced from 4 % (12X1/3) to 8 % (12X2/3), * Cic. Att. 4, 15, 7.— In gen., two thirds of any whole. Of shares in a partnership: Nerva constituit, ut tu ex triente socius esses, ego ex besse, Dig. 17, 2, 76.— Of a sum of money: exsolvere bessem pretii, Dig. 17, 1, 12.— Of a tract of land: emere bessem fundi, Dig. 16, 21, 2, § 39: bisque novem, Nemeaee, dabis, bessemque (i. e. eight months) sub illis, Manil. 3, 367.— Of a jugerum: partes duae tertiae pedes decem novem milia et ducentos, hoc est bes, in quo sunt scripula CXCII., Col. 5, 1, 11.— Of a measure of capacity: bes sextarii, Scrib. Comp. 126.— Of a pound, = 8 ounces: in binos semodios farinae satis esse bessem fermenti, Plin. 18, 11, 26, § 102; Scrib. Comp. 157.— Of an inheritance: heres ex besse, Plin. Ep. 7, 24, 2.— Meton. for eight: quincunces et sex cyathos bessemque bibamus, Caïus ut fiat Julius et Proculus (i. e. so many letters were comprised in these names; cf. 1. bibo, 2. e.), Mart. 11, 36, 7 and 8.— Bes alter = (12+8)/12 = 1 2/3, Fest. s. v. triens, p. 363 Müll.— In mathematics, where the cardinal number is six (cf. as !*?), bes = 4, Gr. δίμοιρος, Vitr. 3, 1, p. 61 Rod. and bes alter = (6+4)/6 = 1 2/3, Gr. ἐπιδίμοιρος, id. ib.

greek_sentence: [3.1.7] Non minus etiam, quod pes hominis altitudinis sextam habet partem, (ita etiam, ex eo quod perficitur pedum numero corporis altitudo, veteribus columnis basis scapi elata sexies altitudines terminavit) eum perfectum constituerunt, cubitumque animadverterunt ex sex palmis constare digitisque XXIIII .
english_sentence_A: [3.1.7] No less also, because the foot of a man has the sixth part of his height (so too, from the fact that the height of the body is completed by the number of feet, in the ancient columns the base of the shaft, raised sixfold, delimited the heights), they established it as perfect, and they observed that the cubit consists of six palms and twenty-four digits.
english_sentence_B: [3.1.7] No less also, because a man's foot is the sixth part of his height (and so too, from the fact that the height of the body is completed by the number of feet, the base of the shaft in ancient columns, raised six times, determined their heights), they established that number as perfect, and they observed that the cubit consists of six palms and twenty-four digits.

greek_sentence: ex eo etiam videntur civitates Graecorum fecisse, quemadmodum cubitus est sex palmorum, in drachma, qua nummo uterentur, aereos signatos uti asses ex aequo sex, quos obolos appellant, quadrantesque obolorum, quae alii dichalca, nonnulli trichalca dicunt, pro digitis viginti quattuor in drachma constituisse.
english_sentence_A: From this too the cities of the Greeks seem to have done likewise: just as the cubit is of six palms, so in the drachma, which they used as a coin, they seem to have established six stamped bronze pieces, like asses, in equal shares, which they call obols, and the quarter-parts of obols, which some call dichalca and some trichalca, in place of the twenty-four digits in the drachma.
english_sentence_B: From this, too, the states of the Greeks seem to have acted likewise: just as the cubit is of six palms, so in the drachma, which they used as coin, they established stamped bronze pieces, like asses, six of equal value, which they call obols; and quarters of obols, which some call dichalka and others trichalka, they established to the number of twenty-four in the drachma, corresponding to the digits.

greek_sentence: altitudo ita uti atticurges; item et eius plinthos; reliquumque praeter plinthum, quod erit tertia pars crassitudinis columnae, dividatur in partes septem: inde trium partium torus, qui est in summo; reliquae quattuor partes dividendae sunt aequaliter, et una pars fiat cum suis astragalis et supercilio superior trochilus, altera pars inferiori trochilo relinquatur; sed inferior maior apparebit, ideo quod habebit ad extremam plinthum proiecturam.
english_sentence_A: The height as for the Attic; likewise also its plinth; and the remainder, apart from the plinth, which will be a third part of the thickness of the column, is to be divided into seven parts: of these, the torus which is at the top is of three parts; the remaining four parts are to be divided equally, and let one part, with its astragals and its supercilium, be made the upper trochilus, and let the other part be left for the lower trochilus; but the lower will appear larger, because it will have a projection out to the edge of the plinth.
english_sentence_B: The height is to be as in the Attic type, and likewise its plinth; and let the remainder apart from the plinth, which will be a third part of the thickness of the column, be divided into seven parts: of these, three parts go to the torus which is at the top; the remaining four parts are to be divided equally, and let one part, together with its astragals and the overhanging fillet, form the upper trochilus, and let the other part be left to the lower trochilus; but the lower will appear larger, because it will have a projection out to the edge of the plinth.

greek_sentence: [3.5.4] Spiris perfectis et conlocatis columnae sunt medianae in pronao et postico ad perpendiculum medii centri conlocandae, angulares autem quaeque e regione earum futurae sunt in lateribus aedis dextra ac sinistra, uti partes interiores, quae ad parietes cellae spectant, ad perpendiculum latus habeant conlocatum, exteriores autem partes †uti dicant se earum contracturam.
english_sentence_A: [3.5.4] When the bases have been completed and set in place, the middle columns in the pronaos and in the posticum are to be set up on the perpendicular of their central axis, but the corner ones, and each of those that are to stand in line with them on the sides of the temple, to right and to left, in such a way that the inner parts, which look toward the walls of the cella, have their side set on the perpendicular, while the outer parts †so as to declare† their own contraction.

greek_sentence: Capitulis perfectis, deinde in scapis columnarum non ad libellam sed ad aequalem modulum conlocatis, ut, quae adiectio in stylobatis facta fuerit, in superioribus membris respondeat , epistyliorum ratio sic est habenda, uti, si columnae fuerint a minima XII pedum ad quindecim pedes, epistylii sit altitudo dimidia crassitudinis imae columnae; item si ab XV pedibus ad XX , columnae altitudo dimetiatur in partes tredecim, et unius partis altitudo epistylii fiat; item si XX ad XXV pedes, dividatur altitudo in partes XII et semissem, et eius una pars epistylium in altitudine fiat; item si ab XXV pedibus ad XXX , dividatur in partes XII , et eius una pars altitudo fiat.
english_sentence_A: When the capitals have been finished, and then set upon the shafts of the columns, not to a level but to an equal module, so that the addition which has been made in the stylobates may correspond in the upper members, the proportion of the epistyles is to be reckoned thus: if the columns are from the smallest, of 12 feet, up to fifteen feet, let the height of the epistyle be half the thickness of the bottom of the column; likewise if from 15 feet to 20, let the height of the column be measured out into thirteen parts, and let the height of the epistyle be made one part; likewise if from 20 to 25 feet, let the height be divided into 12 parts and a half, and let the epistyle be made one part of it in height; likewise if from 25 feet to 30, let it be divided into 12 parts, and let the height be made one part of it.
english_sentence_B: Likewise, if from fifteen feet to twenty, let the height of the column be measured off into thirteen parts, and let the height of the architrave be made one part. Likewise, if from twenty to twenty-five feet, let the height be divided into twelve parts and a half, and let one part of it be made the architrave in height.

greek_sentence: Capitulis perfectis, deinde in scapis columnarum non ad libellam sed ad aequalem modulum conlocatis, ut, quae adiectio in stylobatis facta fuerit, in superioribus membris respondeat , epistyliorum ratio sic est habenda, uti, si columnae fuerint a minima XII pedum ad quindecim pedes, epistylii sit altitudo dimidia crassitudinis imae columnae; item si ab XV pedibus ad XX , columnae altitudo dimetiatur in partes tredecim, et unius partis altitudo epistylii fiat; item si XX ad XXV pedes, dividatur altitudo in partes XII et semissem, et eius una pars epistylium in altitudine fiat; item si ab XXV pedibus ad XXX , dividatur in partes XII , et eius una pars altitudo fiat.
english_sentence_A: When the capitals have been finished, and then set upon the shafts of the columns, not to a level but to an equal module, so that the addition which has been made in the stylobates may correspond in the upper members, the proportion of the epistyles is to be reckoned thus: if the columns are from the smallest, of 12 feet, up to fifteen feet, let the height of the epistyle be half the thickness of the bottom of the column; likewise if from 15 feet to 20, let the height of the column be measured out into thirteen parts, and let the height of the epistyle be made one part; likewise if from 20 to 25 feet, let the height be divided into 12 parts and a half, and let the epistyle be made one part of it in height; likewise if from 25 feet to 30, let it be divided into 12 parts, and let the height be made one part of it.
english_sentence_B: Likewise, if from fifteen feet to twenty, let the height of the column be measured off into thirteen parts, and let the height of the architrave be made one part. Likewise, if from twenty to twenty-five feet, let the height be divided into twelve parts and a half, and let one part of it be made the architrave in height.

english_sentence_A: [3.5.9] For the higher the sight of the eye climbs, the less easily does it cut through the density of the air; and so, dissipated by the extent of the height and stripped of its strength, it reports to the senses an uncertain quantity of the modules.

greek_sentence: haec autem, quae erunt contra columnas, perterebrata sint ad canalem, qui excipit e tegulis aquam caelestem; mediana autem sint solida, uti, quae cadit vis aquae per tegulas in canalem, ne deiciatur per intercolumnia neque transeuntes perfundat, sed quae sunt contra columnas, videantur emittere vomentia ructus aquarum ex ore.
english_sentence_A: Those, however, which will be opposite the columns are to be bored through to the channel which receives the rainwater from the tiles; but the intermediate ones are to be solid, so that the mass of water which falls through the tiles into the channel is not thrown down through the intercolumniations and does not drench those passing by, but those which are opposite the columns may appear to vomit forth gushes of water from their mouths.
english_sentence_B: Those, moreover, which will be opposite the columns are to be bored through to the channel that receives the rainwater from the tiles; but the middle ones are to be solid, so that the force of water that falls through the tiles into the channel may not be thrown down through the intercolumniations nor drench those passing by, while those that are opposite the columns may appear to emit, vomiting, belchings of water from the mouth.
